strengths: Addresses an important practical setting: unlearning using only the pretrained model and forget set, without retained or auxiliary data. The target-versus-nontarget sensitivity objective is simple and offers a useful direction beyond existing smoothing approaches.

Strong reported class-level results: average accuracy gaps from retraining are 0.07 percentage points on CIFAR-100 and 0.15 on Tiny ImageNet. Several subclass results are also competitive with retained-data-dependent methods, with substantial runtime savings against baselines such as SalUn.

The evaluation includes six datasets, multiple architectures, numerous baselines, five-trial reporting, sequential deletion, and component ablations. The joint-objective ablation provides useful evidence for the method’s design. A public code link and substantial implementation details support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical connection is not established (Section 3.2). For vector-valued logits, differentiating g(x)^T g(x_i)q with respect to its two inputs yields different contractions, g^T g' q and (g')^T g q; these need not coincide at x=x_i, contrary to the asserted C_k=S_k identity. The derivation also discards training-trajectory and softmax derivatives, and Appendix D does not bound the accumulated cross-sample residual. Input-perturbation sensitivity is additionally distinct from deletion influence. Equation (A7) has another substantive error: it omits the softmax-derivative contribution to cross-entropy curvature.

The broad utility-preservation and superiority claims exceed the evidence. In Table A8, MU-Mis obtains 57.37% test accuracy versus 84.45% for retraining, with an average gap of 19.85 versus RUM’s 0.84. For highly memorized samples, Table A16 reports retained accuracy of 66.79% versus 100% for retraining. Even in standard random-subset experiments, Table A7 shows worse utility gaps than SCAR on CIFAR-10 and JiT on SVHN. These substantial limitations deserve prominent treatment in the abstract and main conclusions.

The practical stopping and tuning claims are insufficiently supported. Actual thresholds range from 0.68 to 3.0 and reach 10 in sequential experiments, whereas the sensitivity study only examines 0.7–1.0 on one task. Appendix F.4 introduces task-dependent reweighting with kappa=80 and fixes c'=1 for random-subset deletion, which needs reconciliation with the requirement c'!=c. Random-subset hyperparameters and a selection procedure demonstrably independent of retained-data or retraining feedback are missing.

Privacy conclusions are stronger than the attack evidence warrants. MIA-Entropy measures the fraction classified as members; reducing this fraction below retraining does not establish indistinguishability or successful deletion. The additional SCRUB-LiRA evaluation is useful, but random-subset scores remain 52.66±0.40 for MU-Mis versus 49.68±0.30 for retraining. Attack construction, calibration, and performance at low false-positive rates need fuller reporting before claiming reliable privacy protection.

Material numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation. For CIFAR-10 random-subset deletion, MU-Mis’s MIA-Entropy is 33.04 in Table A7 but 83.34 in Table A11, without an explained protocol change. Table A8’s KL_All value of 0.7509 also does not reconcile with the reported subset KL values and Equation (A4)’s dataset-wide averaging under the stated forget-set sizes. These discrepancies directly affect the privacy and output-indistinguishability claims.

The ethics statement says no personally identifiable information is used, despite experiments on an identifiable-face recognition dataset. This statement should be corrected, with dataset provenance and permitted use explained.
